<reason>A close, high-quality debate. A built a genuinely strong CON case: reframing the metric as timely care, the Canada queue evidence, the monopsony supply squeeze, and the recession concentration-of-risk point, plus a real unanswered hit (A4.4) that visible Canadian queues persist for decades despite B's "democratic accountability" mechanism. But B controlled the decisive interpretive and structural clash. B's reading of the motion — it targets employer systems *that tie access to work*, with the US as the paradigm CON case — survived A's falsifiability question, and B's conduit/floor-net frame absorbed nearly every A concession: subsidized continuation, capped cost-sharing, unemployment backstops all turned out to be the state guaranteeing the floor with intermediaries attached. A's own answers kept re-importing government guarantees (even A4.3's German worker relies on unemployment insurance), which B converted into "my side, routed through extra intermediaries." B also won administrative efficiency largely by default. A answered both pressure questions directly and landed sharp discrete hits, but defended a hypothetical patched system rather than the motion's comparator, never engaged the efficiency point, and lost the end of a turn to clipping. B made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 (B2.1–B2.2): turning A's centerpiece Germany example into the convergence thesis — the employer there is a billing conduit because the state guarantees the floor, so single-payer is "that guarantee without a thousand intermediaries." This move defined the rest of the debate; A's proportionality counter (a cheap net for the few) was a real answer, but every patch A proposed kept confirming the frame. A's best counter-hit — that decades of visible Canadian queues disprove the accountability mechanism (A4.4) — was never squarely answered, which keeps the margin moderate.</best_rebuttal>
